sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Say the last appointment you made and one thing you will do next week.
sections.lede: Say each line aloud once. This section is not scored.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: These are the three things you will be able to do by the end of the lesson.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Make appointments, describe symptoms and talk about plans with the present tense and werden.

blocks.text: To make an appointment, use “Ich möchte einen Termin vereinbaren” or “Ich brauche einen Termin”. To move or cancel one, say “Ich muss den Termin verschieben” or “Ich muss den Termin leider absagen”.

At the doctor, describe symptoms with “Ich habe Schmerzen” or “Mir tut der Kopf weh”. For future plans, German often uses the present tense with a time word: Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. Werden + infinitive is also common for predictions and plans.

blocks.title: Polite on the phone
blocks.text: Open with “Guten Tag, mein Name ist …” and close with “Vielen Dank, auf Wiederhören.” These two lines make almost any appointment call sound natural.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

items: Use einen Termin for the direct object of vereinbaren.
Mir tut … weh is a common way to name pain: Mir tut der Rücken weh.
Werden + infinitive is useful for predictions: Es wird morgen regnen.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Listen once, then read the example aloud.

items.example: Ich habe morgen einen Termin beim Arzt.
items.exampleEn: I have a doctor’s appointment tomorrow.
I have had pain since yesterday.

items.example: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Köln.
items.exampleEn: I am buying a ticket to Cologne.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Notice how the pattern behaves in a complete sentence.

items.en: I would like to make an appointment.
items.note: The standard opening on the phone.

items.de: Können wir den Termin auf Freitag verschieben?
items.en: Can we move the appointment to Friday?
items.note: Verschieben means to move to another time.
The dative mir names the person in pain.

items.en: Tomorrow I am travelling to Berlin.
items.note: The present tense plus morgen expresses a future plan.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

items.hint: The sch is one sound: SHMER-tsen.

blocks.text: In Germany, you usually need an appointment for a doctor, and many practices ask you to call ahead. “Akutsprechstunde” is a slot for urgent cases without an appointment, but it is not a guarantee.
Punctuality matters. Arrive a few minutes early and bring your insurance card (“Versichertenkarte”). If you cannot come, cancel as early as possible; repeated no-shows can lead to a fee.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: Read the scene, then play it and follow the speakers.
sections.setting: Nora calls a doctor’s practice on Monday morning.

lines.speaker: Nora
lines.de: Guten Tag, ich möchte einen Termin vereinbaren.
lines.en: Hello, I would like to make an appointment.

lines.speaker: Praxis
lines.de: Waren Sie schon einmal bei uns?
lines.en: Have you been to us before?

lines.speaker: Nora
lines.de: Ja. Ich habe seit gestern Schmerzen im Rücken.
lines.en: Yes. I have had back pain since yesterday.

lines.speaker: Praxis
lines.de: Kommen Sie bitte morgen um neun Uhr.
lines.en: Please come tomorrow at nine o’clock.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Talking about appointments and plans
sections.lede: Use polite fixed phrases for appointments and the present tense for near-future plans.

blocks.text: Werden + infinitive is another future form: Ich werde morgen zum Arzt gehen. At A2, the present tense with a time word is usually simpler and more natural.

sections.tip: Learn the phone opening and closing as fixed chunks. They carry most of the politeness in the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Build: “I would like to make an appointment.”
exercises.explanation: The modal möchte is second and the infinitive is at the end.
Mir is the dative person, and weh tut closes the sentence.

exercises.explanation: The time phrase comes first, so the verb follows immediately.

The practice says “Kommen Sie heute um drei Uhr.”

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Call a practice, describe one symptom and arrange an appointment for tomorrow.

model.de: Guten Tag, mein Name ist Anna Klein. Ich habe Schmerzen im Bein. Ich möchte einen Termin vereinbaren. Geht es morgen um zehn Uhr?
model.en: Hello, my name is Anna Klein. I have pain in my leg. I would like to make an appointment. Is tomorrow at ten possible?

tips: Open with your name and the reason for the call.
Use “Ich habe Schmerzen” or “Mir tut … weh”.
Ask for a specific time with “Geht es …?” to sound natural.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.why: After a modal verb, use the infinitive.
German normally uses the plural Schmerzen for pain.
When the time phrase comes first, the verb stays in second position.
